newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UBS says Holocaust fund makes business sense.
newsitem.headline: UBS says Holocaust fund makes business sense.

text.p: Union Bank of Switzerland on Thursday cited worries that a U.S. backlash could hurt its business as part of the reason it joined Switzerland's other biggest banks to create a Holocaust memorial fund.

UBS chairman Robert Studer told shareholders there were business reasons as well as humanitarian motives in donating 100 million Swiss francs together with rivals Credit Suisse Group and Swiss Bank Corp (SBC).

The three banks in February were the first to donate money for a humanitarian fund for Holocaust survivors that the Swiss government then formally created using the cash and another 165 million francs from private companies and the central bank.
"As shareholders of the bank you may be asking yourselves how we can justify this kind of donation," Studer said at the annual shareholder meeting.

The donation was a gesture of good will, he said, "but we are not about to conceal the fact that this gesture is also strongly motivated by our business activities in the U.S., which are important for the overall performance of UBS," Studer said.
"Our position there (the U.S.) and our reputation, on which banking relationships are largely based, are at stake and are being increasingly called into question," he said.
"While our contribution to the humanitarian fund is certainly justifiable on ethical and moral grounds, there is also a business rationale to it," Studer added.

The memorial fund and broader government plan to create a seven billion Swiss franc foundation to help the world's poor and persecuted came about in the past two months under mounting pressure led by U.S.-based Jewish groups and U.S. politicians.

At the crux of the controversy are Jewish claims that Swiss banks withheld accounts left by Holocaust victims and that Switzerland generally profited from its status as a neutral financial centre during World War Two.

New York city and state considered barring public business with Swiss banks and other state and local authorities have voiced similar threats, although the World Jewish Congress (WJC) dropped boycott plans after the Holocaust fund was created.
SBC said in its monthly magazine this week that the step helped convince even Swiss banks' most vociferous critics that the secretive institutions were adopting a constructive stance.

"SBC sees its contribution here as a humanitarian act that should show it wants to depart from the legalistic and what was sometimes perceived as a hard-hearted way of treating Holocaust victims after World War Two," it wrote.

UBS chief executive Mathis Cabiallavetta used the bank's shareholder meeting to apologise again for UBS's shredding of documents from the bank's archives relating to war-era history of its Eidgenossische Bank unit, which it bought in 1945.
"The destruction of the documents was only possible due to a whole series of mistakes following disastrously one on top of the other," he said in the text of a spech to shareholders.
Cabiallavetta said the shredding -- uncovered by a suspicious night watchman -- was "an error which seriously damaged our reputation".

But he noted that Swiss banking regulators and an independent panel formed by Jewish groups and Swiss bankers to search for any dormant Jewish wealth had found the shredding was not part of a deliberate policy by UBS management.
"I would like to use this opportunity to once again apologise for the incident," he said.
